reason: The sources corroborate over a dozen atomic facts detailing Stickney crater's massive scale, the near-destruction of Phobos, and competing explanations for the moon's grooves.
story: Mars's tiny, potato-shaped moon Phobos carries an enormous scar: Stickney crater. Measuring nine kilometers across on a moon only twenty-seven kilometers wide, the impact crater occupies nearly half the moon's width. The ancient asteroid collision was so colossal that it nearly blasted Phobos into rubble. The moon only survived because its interior is highly porous, soaking up the catastrophic shockwaves like a sponge. When NASA missions like Mariner and Viking first photographed Phobos in the 1970s, they revealed strange grooves scouring the moon's surface. Planetary scientists have debated their cause for decades: some models show giant boulders blasted from the Stickney impact rolling and bouncing completely around the tiny moon, while other models suggest Mars's gravity is pulling Phobos apart, producing stress fractures across its surface. In tens of millions of years, Mars will finish what the Stickney impact started, tearing Phobos to pieces.
angle: An impact carved a nine-kilometer crater into a moon just twenty-seven kilometers wide, and the moon only survived the cataclysm because its interior was as porous as a sponge.

claims.claim: Stickney is the largest impact crater on the Martian moon Phobos.
Stickney crater measures approximately 9 kilometers in diameter.
Phobos is an irregular, potato-shaped or oblong moon.
Phobos measures about 27 kilometers across at its longest or widest dimension.
The crater is named after Chloe Angeline Stickney Hall, wife of Phobos discoverer Asaph Hall.
The impact that formed Stickney was so violent it nearly destroyed or shattered Phobos.
Phobos's high porosity or sponge-like low density cushioned the shock and prevented the moon from being shattered.
NASA spacecraft including Mariner and Viking first imaged Phobos's surface grooves in the 1970s.
A network of linear grooves and fractures runs across the surface of Phobos.
Computer simulations show boulders blasted from Stickney could have rolled across Phobos to carve its grooves.
Due to Phobos's weak gravity, rolling boulders could have traveled entirely around the moon.
Another scientific hypothesis suggests Phobos's surface grooves are caused by tidal forces exerted by Mars.
Researchers have also proposed that grooves were created by debris ejected from impacts on Mars.
The interior of Phobos is modeled as a low-density, fragile rubble pile.
The walls of Stickney crater show lineations caused by landslides of falling material.
Stickney crater exhibits a light bluish spectral coloration along its rim or edge.
Phobos is being drawn closer to Mars over time and will eventually be torn apart.
Japan's Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission plans to study Phobos and collect surface samples.

disputed: Origin of the surface grooves: researchers disagree whether they were created by boulders rolling from Stickney, tidal deformation from Mars, or debris ejected from Mars impacts; the script should attribute each view rather than stating one as definitive fact.

Age of Stickney crater: models suggest either 4.2 billion years ago under a Mars giant-impact model or 2.6 billion years ago under an asteroid-capture model; the script should state that estimates range between 2.6 and 4.2 billion years depending on Phobos's origin.

Moon diameter measurements: sources cite 27 km across at Phobos's widest point while another cites a mean diameter of roughly 22.2 km; the script should distinguish the maximum dimension from the mean diameter.
